title: G-Merging: Graph Model Merging for Multi-Task Knowledge Consolidation
one_liner: When you train separate graph models on separate tasks, G-Merging combines them into one efficient model by routing each input graph to the right task specialist based on its structure.
lead: Machine learning teams often train separate models, each specialized for one task. But keeping many models is wasteful — they use lots of memory and computing power. G-Merging solves this by merging multiple graph models (trained on different graph tasks) into one efficient model that still performs as well as separate models. The trick: instead of treating all graphs the same, it routes each graph to the right specialist based its structure.

problem.h2: Why merging regular models fails on graphs
paras: Suppose you have two different graph tasks: predicting disease spread on social networks, and predicting fraud on transaction networks. You train one graph model on disease, another on fraud. Each works perfectly for its task, but now you're storing two entire models in memory.

A beginner tries the obvious fix: just average the two models' weights together. This sometimes works for regular images and text, but fails badly on graphs. Why? Graphs have a hidden structure — the shape of connections matters as much as the numbers. When you average weights blindly, you smash together models that expect completely different graph shapes, and you lose the specialized knowledge each one learned.
The paper calls this the unique structural heterogeneity problem: different graph tasks have fundamentally different patterns of how things connect. Averaging weights ignores that.

callout.html: G-Merging merges multiple specialized graph models into one by routing each input graph to the expert that matches its structure best.

steps.text: Average weights of fine-tuned models to capture shared knowledge.
For each task, calculate how graph structure differs (using Wasserstein distance on the learned patterns inside the model).
Train lightweight fix-up layers (adapters) to restore task-specific patterns.
Create a router that scores how well each input graph matches each task's structure.
When a new graph arrives, send it to whichever adapter fits its structure best.

paras: G-Merging changes which specialized model (which adapter) handles each graph. Instead of using one merged model for everything, it dynamically picks the right specialist based on the graph's shape.

hidden.h2: Structural similarity: which adapter fits this graph?
hidden.name: structural similarity score
paras: G-Merging measures how similar an input graph is to the graph structure each model was trained on. This is a single score for each graph-to-task pair, showing how well that task's specialist fits this particular input.

The paper estimates this using Wasserstein distance: a way to measure how different two distributions are. It compares the learned embeddings (the internal patterns the merged model found) to the embeddings from the original task-specific model. A small distance means the graph structure matches; a large distance means it does not.

heat.caption: Darker means higher structural similarity. This graph should go to the expert with the darkest cell.

reads.html: Structural similarity is a score from 0 to 1 that says how much this input graph's shape matches what each specialist model expects. High score means route here; low score means route elsewhere.

Topology-aware Wasserstein Distance (TWD) measures divergence between the embeddings of the merged model and the original task-specific fine-tuned model on the given input. Lower TWD indicates structural alignment.

mechanism.h2: Why routing by structure fixes the merging problem
paras: The core problem: when you average two models trained on different graph structures, the average model is confused — it does not know if it should expect dense clusters or chain-like patterns, local communities or global structure. So it performs poorly on both.

G-Merging fixes this by doing three things. First, it merges the models coarsely (averaging weights) to capture shared knowledge, so the merged model learns common graph patterns. Second, it trains tiny adapters for each task: these are small neural networks that take the merged model's output and adjust it to restore the task-specific patterns the original model learned. The adapters are trained using Wasserstein distance, which measures graph-embedding similarity directly — so each adapter learns exactly which adjustments fix the structure for its task.

Third, instead of running all inputs through the merged model plus all adapters, it builds a router that looks at the input graph's structure and chooses just one adapter to apply. This routing happens fast (no training needed) because it is based on whether the input structure matches each adapter's specialty. A dense graph goes to the dense-specialist adapter; a sparse graph goes to the sparse-specialist. Because the right adapter is always chosen, the merged model performs almost as well as separate models but uses far less memory.

items.html: If two tasks both work on dense social networks with the same clustering pattern, the router may route the same graph to both adapters equally. The method assumes task structures differ in real ways; it struggles when they overlap.

If a real social network becomes sparser over time (people disconnect), the router's similarity scores were learned on old structure patterns. It may route wrong, sending sparse graphs to a dense-trained adapter.

items.b: The Wasserstein distance metric is expensive.
items.html: Computing Wasserstein distance requires comparing learned patterns in detail. For very large graphs or many tasks, this routing step slows down the time to answer.

G-Merging works well when task structures genuinely differ, when you have labeled data to measure structural similarity, and when the adapter overhead is smaller than the savings from sharing one merged model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy dataset: three small graph classification tasks (e.g., sparse social graph, dense citation graph, chain-structured transaction graph). Train one model on each. Merge them using G-Merging (average weights, add adapters, build the structure-aware router). Then test: for each task's test graphs, measure how often the router sends it to the correct adapter. Measure accuracy on each task. Measure total model size.
demo.metric_eq: routing_accuracy = (graphs sent to correct adapter) / (total test graphs); task_accuracy = correct_predictions / total_predictions; model_size_ratio = merged_size / (3 * individual_size)
demo.closing: The demo should make impossible to miss: routing scores align with task structure (sparse graphs hit the sparse adapter), and the merged model matches single-task accuracy while using one-third the memory.
